content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In Christian teaching, the field most commonly symbolizes the world — the whole realm of humanity in which God's kingdom is sown, where good and evil grow together until the final judgment/harvest. This meaning is treated as authoritative because Jesus himself supplies it in his explanation of the parable of the wheat and the tares: 'The field is the world' (Matthew 13:38). Closely bound to this is the derivative missionary sense: the world as a harvest field of souls ready to be gathered.","primary_basis":["Matthew 13:24-30, 36-43 (parable of the wheat and the tares; v. 38 'the field is the world')","Matthew 9:37-38 ('the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few')","John 4:35 ('lift up your eyes and look on the fields, for they are white already to harvest')","Luke 10:2 (Lord of the harvest sending laborers)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"The mission field: the world's population viewed as a harvest of souls awaiting evangelism; the basis of the widespread evangelical idiom 'the mission field.'","basis":["John 4:35","Matthew 9:37-38","Luke 10:2"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The church or believers as God's cultivated field — God's people under his husbandry, tended by ministers who plant and water while God gives the growth.","basis":["1 Corinthians 3:6-9 ('you are God's field, God's building')"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The human heart as soil/ground receiving the seed of the word — strictly the 'soils' of the parable of the sower, but often merged with field imagery in preaching.","basis":["Matthew 13:3-23","Mark 4:3-20","Luke 8:4-15"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The field containing hidden treasure as the world in which Christ purchases his treasured people (or, alternately, the field as the sphere in which the believer finds the kingdom).","basis":["Matthew 13:44"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Fields as covenant land/inheritance and redemption imagery (kinsman-redeemer purchase of fields), read typologically of Christ's redemption.","basis":["Jeremiah 32:6-15 (Jeremiah buys the field at Anathoth)","Ruth 4:1-10","Leviticus 25:23-28"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"The 'Field of Blood' (Akeldama) as a symbol of the wages of betrayal and sin.","basis":["Matthew 27:3-10","Acts 1:18-19"],"prominence":"rare"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"The consensus is unusually firm for the primary meaning because Matthew 13:38 contains an explicit dominical interpretation ('the field is the world'), which commentators across Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and evangelical traditions treat as controlling for that parable. However, 'field' is context-dependent across Scripture: in 1 Corinthians 3:9 it is explicitly the church, and in harvest sayings it functions as the mission field. Historically, the tension between 'the field is the world' (Matthew 13) and 'you are God's field' (1 Corinthians 3) fed the Augustinian/Donatist debate over whether the wheat-and-tares field means the world or the church — Augustine's 'world' reading (following the text) prevailed, though a 'field = church' application persists in some preaching. Note also that the parable-of-the-sower soils describe hearts, not strictly the 'field,' though popular usage conflates them."}
